$$
a\equiv b  \quad \Longleftrightarrow\quad a+c\equiv b+c \qquad (\textrm{mod}\,n).
$$

Similarly, the subtraction property states that

$$
a\equiv b \quad \Longleftrightarrow\quad a-c\equiv b-c \qquad (\textrm{mod}\,n).
$$

We use the subtraction property to subtract $8$ from both sides of the given congruence, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x+8 & ≡11\, & (\text{mod}\,15) \\ x+8-8 & ≡11-8\, & (\text{mod}\,15) \\ x & ≡3\, & (\text{mod}\,15)\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186152059 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-1f9b7d3e-524b-551d-8a94-9d846396890c" "question-c78b30a9-b100-5475-8a11-aa23c310f873" "question-abd575a7-0f26-5465-b126-ff96772a8759" "question-3911df9a-6841-59e6-b534-6e8a3aa2e9ba" "question-6d54f83a-3712-59c6-b238-0e2bb4334321"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186151836 :question/problem "Which of the following numbers is congruent to $0$ modulo $18?$

- $-45$

- $42$

- $-54$" :question/worked-solution "First, recall that  

$$
a \equiv 0 \quad (\textrm{mod}\,n) \qquad \Longleftrightarrow \qquad a = kn,
$$

where $k\in\mathbb Z.$ In other words, when $a$ is divided by $n,$ there is no remainder. This means that any integer multiple of $18$ is congruent to $0$ modulo $18.$

So, since $18\,|\,(-54),$ we obtain

$$
-54 \equiv (-3) \cdot {\color{blue}18} \equiv (-3)\cdot 0\equiv 0 \quad (\text{mod}\:{\color{blue}18}).
$$

None of the other options are multiples of $18.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only."" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186152060 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-bc99e19c-49e9-51e2-8ead-f8afe5651f31" "question-77cbdd5d-15bd-5f9e-950f-9243376a199b" "question-d19c623d-9750-5d15-989b-ed8e917e3481"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186151839 :question/problem "Which of the following is equivalent to $x \equiv 23\: (\textrm{mod}\,6)?$ 

- $x \equiv 2 \quad (\textrm{mod}\,6)$

- $x \equiv 3 \quad (\textrm{mod}\,6)$

- $x \equiv 5 \quad (\textrm{mod}\,6)$" :question/worked-solution "When we add zero to both sides of a congruence modulo $n$, we can form an equivalent congruence by writing zero as an integer multiple of $n.$ This works because every integer multiple of $n$ is congruent to zero modulo $n.$

In our case, we add zero to both sides of the congruence and then use the fact that  ${\color{blue}6} \cdot (-3) \equiv 0 \: (\text{mod}\:{\color{blue}6})$ to rewrite the right-hand side, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x+0 & ≡23+0\, & (\text{mod}\,6) \\ x & ≡23+0\, & (\text{mod}\,6) \\  & ≡23+6\cdot (-3)\, & (\text{mod}\,6) \\  & ≡23-18\, & (\text{mod}\,6) \\  & ≡5\, & (\text{mod}\,6)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only."" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186152061 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-700ec10d-3e3a-58fc-aadf-2fee69932797" "question-50be2be7-4190-59bf-9880-ce7373f52df0" "question-f453d5f9-efe9-5d81-aae2-3ab414bd5f85" "question-83693413-601d-53f0-b546-e5ed9a2ee614"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186151863 :question/worked-solution "We can solve this problem using modular arithmetic.

First, we note the number of complete months between January 1st, 1896, and April 6th, 1896. 

- There were $2$ months with $31$ days (January and March).

- There were $0$ months with $30$ days.

- There was $1$ month with $29$ days (February) since it was a leap year.

Therefore, the number of days $d$ between January 1st and April 6th is given by

$$
d 
= \overbrace{31(2) + 30(0) + 29(1)}^{\textrm{days to April 1st}} + 5.
$$

Now, note that

$$
31 \equiv 3, \qquad 30\equiv 2, \qquad 29\equiv 1 \qquad (\textrm{mod}\, 7).
$$

Therefore, writing the number $d$ modulo $7,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =2(31)+0(30)+1(29)+5 \\  & ≡2(3)+0(2)+1(1)+5\, & (\text{mod}\,7) \\  & ≡6+0+1+5\, & (\text{mod}\,7) \\  & ≡12\, & (\text{mod}\,7) \\  & ≡5\, & (\text{mod}\,7)\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the day of the week is the same as the date $5$ days after January 1st, 1896, namely Monday." :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-23919475-35c0-5151-a80d-eb2f21c5c2a9" :question/id #uuid "23919475-35c0-5151-a80d-eb2f21c5c2a9" :question/math-academy-id "q-79667" :question/problem "Which of the following is equivalent to $x+5≡11\,(\text{mod}\,15)?$" :question/worked-solution "The addition property of congruences states that

$$
a≡b\,⟺\,a+c≡b+c\,(\text{mod}\,n).
$$

Similarly, the subtraction property states that

$$
a≡b\,⟺\,a-c≡b-c\,(\text{mod}\,n).
$$

We use the subtraction property to subtract $5$ from both sides of the given congruence, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x+5 & ≡11\, & (\text{mod}\,15) \\ x+5-5 & ≡11-5\, & (\text{mod}\,15) \\ x & ≡6\, & (\text{mod}\,15)\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-921948e6-4b81-53f0-b19f-76fb55d28b4e"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id :question/math-academy-id "q-213291" :question/problem "A parodic holiday, International Talk Like a Pirate Day, was celebrated for the first time on September 19th, 1995. Given that January 1st, 1995, was a Sunday, use congruences to determine on which day of the week this holiday was celebrated for the first time.

*Hint: The year 1995 was not a leap year since it is not divisible by $4.$*" :question/worked-solution "We can solve this problem using modular arithmetic.

First, we note the number of complete months between January 1st, 1995, and September 1st, 1995. 

- There were $5$ months with $31$ days (January, March, May, July,  and  August).

- There were $2$ months with $30$ days (April and  June).

- There was $1$ month with $28$ days (February).

Therefore, the number of days $d$ between January 1st and September 19th is given by

$$
d=\overset{\text{days to September 1st}}{\overset{⏞}{31(5)+30(2)+28(1)}}+18.
$$

Now, note that

$$
31≡3,\,30≡2,\,28≡0,\,18≡4\,(\text{mod}\,7).
$$

Therefore, writing the number $d$ modulo $7,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =5(31)+2(30)+1(28)+18 \\  & ≡5(3)+2(2)+1(0)+4\, & (\text{mod}\,7) \\  & ≡15+4+0+4\, & (\text{mod}\,7) \\  & ≡1+4+0+4\, & (\text{mod}\,7) \\  & ≡9\, & (\text{mod}\,7) \\  & ≡2\, & (\text{mod}\,7)\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the day of the week is the same as the date $2$ days after January 1st, 1995, namely Tuesday." :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields $$

$$

$$
31≡3,\,30≡2,\,29≡1,\,5≡5,\,(\text{mod}\,7).
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =5(31)+3(30)+1(29)+5 \\  & ≡5(3)+3(2)+(1)+5\, & (\text{mod}\,7) \\  & ≡15+6+1+5\, & (\text{mod}\,7) \\  & ≡1+6+1+5\, & (\text{mod}\,7) \\  & ≡13\, & (\text{mod}\,7) \\  & ≡6\, & (\text{mod}\,7)\end{aligned}

First, we note the number of complete months between January 1st, 2000, and November 1st, 2000. 

- There were $6$ months with $31$ days (January, March, May, July, August, and October).

- There were $3$ months with $30$ days (April, June, and September).

- There was $1$ month with $29$ days (February).

Therefore, the number of days $d$ between January 1st and November 4th is given by

$$
d=\overset{\text{days to November 1st}}{\overset{⏞}{31(6)+30(3)+29(1)}}+3.
$$

Now, note that

$$
31≡3,\,30≡2,\,29≡1,\,(\text{mod}\,7).
$$

Therefore, writing the number $d$ modulo $7,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =6(31)+3(30)+1(29)+3 \\  & ≡6(3)+3(2)+(1)+3\, & (\text{mod}\,7) \\  & ≡18+6+1+3\, & (\text{mod}\,7) \\  & ≡4+6+1+3\, & (\text{mod}\,7) \\  & ≡14\, & (\text{mod}\,7) \\  & ≡0\, & (\text{mod}\,7)\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the day of the week is the same as January 1st, 2000, namely Saturday." :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields $n$, we can form an equivalent congruence by writing zero as an integer multiple of $n.$ This works because every integer multiple of $n$ is congruent to zero modulo $n.$

This gives rise to the following facts:

$$
\begin{aligned}a≡b\,⟺\,a≡b+kn\,(\text{mod}\,n) \\ a≡b\,⟺\,a+kn≡b\,(\text{mod}\,n)\end{aligned}
$$

So, we can add a multiple of the modulus $13$ to one side of the congruence. Notice that 

$$
-26=(-2)\cdot 13.
$$

Therefore, we obtain the following:

Moreover, $a$ and $b$ are congruent modulo $n$ if and only if $n$ divides $a-b.$

$$
a \equiv b \quad (\textrm{mod}\,n) \qquad \Longleftrightarrow \qquad n \mid (a-b) \qquad \Longleftrightarrow \qquad a-b = kn,
$$

where $k\in\mathbb Z.$ 

A convenient property of congruences is that we can add and subtract on both sides, just as with regular equations. 

Consider, for instance, the following true statement:

$$
22\equiv 10 \quad (\textrm{mod}\,12)
$$

The **addition property** allows us to add an integer to both sides. For example, adding $2$ to both sides gives

$$
\begin{aligned}22+2 & ≡10+2\, & (\text{mod}\,12) \\ 24 & ≡12\, & (\text{mod}\,12)\end{aligned}
$$

which is also a true statement since $24$ and $12$ both have a remainder of zero when divided by $12.$

Similarly, the **subtraction property** allows us to subtract an integer from both sides. For example, subtracting $9$ from both sides of our original statement gives

$$
\begin{aligned}22-9 & ≡10-9\, & (\text{mod}\,12) \\ 13 & ≡1\, & (\text{mod}\,12)\end{aligned}
$$

which is a true statement since $13$ and $1$ both have a remainder of $1$ when divided by $12.$

In general, the addition and subtraction properties state the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}a≡b\,⟺\,a+c≡b+c\,(\text{mod}\,n) \\ a≡b\,⟺\,a-c≡b-c\,(\text{mod}\,n)\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186153447 :tutorial/content "According to the definition of modular congruence, we have that

$$
a \equiv b \quad (\textrm{mod}\,n) \qquad \Longleftrightarrow \qquad n \mid (a-b)  \qquad \Longleftrightarrow \qquad a = b+ kn,
$$

where $k \in \mathbb{Z}.$ Substituting $b=0,$ we obtain

$$
a \equiv 0 \quad (\textrm{mod}\,n) \qquad \Longleftrightarrow \qquad n \mid a  \qquad \Longleftrightarrow \qquad a = kn
$$

This gives rise to the following important fact:

*Any integer multiple of $n$ is congruent to $0$ modulo $n.$*

For example, the numbers $10,$ $-25,$ and $75$ are all are all multiples of ${\color{blue}5},$ so they are all congruent to $0$ modulo ${\color{blue}5}\mathbin{:}$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}10 & =2\cdot 5≡0 & \,(\text{mod}\,5) \\ -25 & =(-5)\cdot 5≡0 & \,(\text{mod}\,5) \\ 75 & =15\cdot 5≡0 & \,(\text{mod}\,5)\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186153450 :tutorial/content "Let's try to simplify the right-hand side of the following congruence:

$$
x \equiv 102 \quad (\textrm{mod}\,5)
$$

By "simplify," we mean that we wish to transform the number on the right-hand side to be the smallest possible positive integer. In other words, we want to write

$$
x \equiv r \quad (\textrm{mod}\,5)\qquad\textrm{for}\qquad 0 \leq r < 5.
$$

When we add $0$ to both sides of a congruence modulo $n$, we can form an equivalent congruence by writing $0$ as an integer multiple of $n.$ This works because every integer multiple of $n$ is congruent to $0\:(\textrm{mod}\:{\color{black}n}).$ 

In our case, we add zero to both sides of the congruence and then use the fact that  ${\color{blue}5} \cdot (-20) \equiv 0 \: (\text{mod}\:{\color{blue}5})$ to rewrite the right-hand side, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ≡102\, & (\text{mod}\,5) \\ x+0 & ≡102+0\, & (\text{mod}\,5) \\ x & \text{ }≡102+5\cdot (-20)\, & (\text{mod}\,5) \\ x & ≡102-100\, & (\text{mod}\,5) \\ x & ≡2\, & (\text{mod}\,5)\end{aligned}
$$

We conclude that $x \equiv 102\, (\textrm{mod}\,5)$ is equivalent to $x \equiv 2\, (\textrm{mod}\,5).$

Our answer is correct because $102$ and $2$ both have a remainder of $2$ when divided by $5,$ and $0 \leq  2 < 5.$

**Note:** By the division algorithm, there is exactly one value of $r$ that satisfies

$$
x \equiv r \quad (\textrm{mod}\,n)\qquad\textrm{for}\qquad 0 \leq r < n.
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186153472 :tutorial/content "In this lesson, we've been working with the so-called addition property of modular arithmetic.

$$
a\equiv b  \quad \Longleftrightarrow\quad a+c\equiv b+c \qquad (\textrm{mod}\,n)
$$

It's straightforward to prove the addition property by writing $a\equiv b$ in terms of divisibility:

$$
\begin{aligned}a≡b\,(\text{mod}\,n)\, & ⟺\,a-b=kn \\  & ⟺\,(a+c)-(b+c)=kn \\  & ⟺\,(a+c)≡(b+c)\,(\text{mod}\,n)\end{aligned}
$$

The subtraction property is proved similarly:

$$
\begin{aligned}a≡b\,(\text{mod}\,n)\, & ⟺\,a-b=kn \\  & ⟺\,(a-c)-(b-c)=kn \\  & ⟺\,(a-c)≡(b-c)\,(\text{mod}\,n)\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186152340 :activity/expected-seconds 600.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]}]

{"source" ":org/Math-Academy" "forms" [[:db/retract 17592186152481 :question/answer-fields 17592186149460] [:db/retract 17592186152473 :question/answer-fields 17592186149387] [:db/retract 17592186152473 :question/answer-fields 17592186149383] [:db/retract 17592186152482 :question/answer-fields 17592186149466] {:db/id 17592186152058 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-23919475-35c0-5151-a80d-eb2f21c5c2a9" "question-0b565593-fa14-5d8e-a413-f5f33c1ea21c" "question-f913a8a8-9a07-5f52-8a63-48e2094f05b2" "question-0ae69b79-17cb-5f18-82ec-b83f30862ca1" 17592186152482 "question-5f92504f-2a88-577a-b7ee-007131f73594"] :knowledge-point/title "Simplifying Congruences" :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186151834 :question/problem "If $x + 8 \equiv 11\: (\textrm{mod}\,15),$ find an equivalent statement where $x$ is isolated." :question/worked-solution "The addition property of congruences states that 

$$
a\equiv b  \quad \Longleftrightarrow\quad a+c\equiv b+c \qquad (\textrm{mod}\,n).
$$

Similarly, the subtraction property states that

$$
a\equiv b \quad \Longleftrightarrow\quad a-c\equiv b-c \qquad (\textrm{mod}\,n).
$$

We use the subtraction property to subtract $8$ from both sides of the given congruence, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x+8 & ≡11\, & (\text{mod}\,15) \\ x+8-8 & ≡11-8\, & (\text{mod}\,15) \\ x & ≡3\, & (\text{mod}\,15)\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186152059 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-1f9b7d3e-524b-551d-8a94-9d846396890c" "question-c78b30a9-b100-5475-8a11-aa23c310f873" "question-abd575a7-0f26-5465-b126-ff96772a8759" "question-3911df9a-6841-59e6-b534-6e8a3aa2e9ba" "question-6d54f83a-3712-59c6-b238-0e2bb4334321"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186151836 :question/problem "Which of the following numbers is congruent to $0$ modulo $18?$

- $-45$

- $42$

- $-54$" :question/worked-solution "First, recall that  

$$
a \equiv 0 \quad (\textrm{mod}\,n) \qquad \Longleftrightarrow \qquad a = kn,
$$

where $k\in\mathbb Z.$ In other words, when $a$ is divided by $n,$ there is no remainder. This means that any integer multiple of $18$ is congruent to $0$ modulo $18.$

So, since $18\,|\,(-54),$ we obtain

$$
-54 \equiv (-3) \cdot {\color{blue}18} \equiv (-3)\cdot 0\equiv 0 \quad (\text{mod}\:{\color{blue}18}).
$$

None of the other options are multiples of $18.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only."" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186152060 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-bc99e19c-49e9-51e2-8ead-f8afe5651f31" "question-77cbdd5d-15bd-5f9e-950f-9243376a199b" "question-d19c623d-9750-5d15-989b-ed8e917e3481"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186151839 :question/problem "Which of the following is equivalent to $x \equiv 23\: (\textrm{mod}\,6)?$ 

- $x \equiv 2 \quad (\textrm{mod}\,6)$

- $x \equiv 3 \quad (\textrm{mod}\,6)$

- $x \equiv 5 \quad (\textrm{mod}\,6)$" :question/worked-solution "When we add zero to both sides of a congruence modulo $n$, we can form an equivalent congruence by writing zero as an integer multiple of $n.$ This works because every integer multiple of $n$ is congruent to zero modulo $n.$

In our case, we add zero to both sides of the congruence and then use the fact that  ${\color{blue}6} \cdot (-3) \equiv 0 \: (\text{mod}\:{\color{blue}6})$ to rewrite the right-hand side, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x+0 & ≡23+0\, & (\text{mod}\,6) \\ x & ≡23+0\, & (\text{mod}\,6) \\  & ≡23+6\cdot (-3)\, & (\text{mod}\,6) \\  & ≡23-18\, & (\text{mod}\,6) \\  & ≡5\, & (\text{mod}\,6)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only."" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186152061 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-700ec10d-3e3a-58fc-aadf-2fee69932797" "question-50be2be7-4190-59bf-9880-ce7373f52df0" "question-f453d5f9-efe9-5d81-aae2-3ab414bd5f85" "question-83693413-601d-53f0-b546-e5ed9a2ee614"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186151863 :question/worked-solution "We can solve this problem using modular arithmetic.

First, we note the number of complete months between January 1st, 1896, and April 6th, 1896. 

- There were $2$ months with $31$ days (January and March).

- There were $0$ months with $30$ days.

- There was $1$ month with $29$ days (February) since it was a leap year.

Therefore, the number of days $d$ between January 1st and April 6th is given by

$$
d 
= \overbrace{31(2) + 30(0) + 29(1)}^{\textrm{days to April 1st}} + 5.
$$

Now, note that

$$
31 \equiv 3, \qquad 30\equiv 2, \qquad 29\equiv 1 \qquad (\textrm{mod}\, 7).
$$

Therefore, writing the number $d$ modulo $7,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =2(31)+0(30)+1(29)+5 \\  & ≡2(3)+0(2)+1(1)+5\, & (\text{mod}\,7) \\  & ≡6+0+1+5\, & (\text{mod}\,7) \\  & ≡12\, & (\text{mod}\,7) \\  & ≡5\, & (\text{mod}\,7)\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the day of the week is the same as the date $5$ days after January 1st, 1896, namely Monday." :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-23919475-35c0-5151-a80d-eb2f21c5c2a9" :question/id #uuid "23919475-35c0-5151-a80d-eb2f21c5c2a9" :question/math-academy-id "q-79667" :question/problem "Which of the following is equivalent to $x+5≡11\,(\text{mod}\,15)?$" :question/worked-solution "The addition property of congruences states that

$$
a≡b\,⟺\,a+c≡b+c\,(\text{mod}\,n).
$$

Similarly, the subtraction property states that

$$
a≡b\,⟺\,a-c≡b-c\,(\text{mod}\,n).
$$

We use the subtraction property to subtract $5$ from both sides of the given congruence, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x+5 & ≡11\, & (\text{mod}\,15) \\ x+5-5 & ≡11-5\, & (\text{mod}\,15) \\ x & ≡6\, & (\text{mod}\,15)\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-921948e6-4b81-53f0-b19f-76fb55d28b4e"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id $$
a≡0\,(\text{mod}\,n)\,⟺\,a=kn,
$$

where $k\in Z.$ In other words, when $a$ is divided by $n,$ there is no remainder. This means that any integer multiple of $4$ is congruent to $0$ modulo $4.$

Therefore, since $4\,|\,52,$ we obtain

$$

:question/math-academy-id "q-213291" :question/problem "A parodic holiday, International Talk Like a Pirate Day, was celebrated for the first time on September 19th, 1995. Given that January 1st, 1995, was a Sunday, use congruences to determine on which day of the week this holiday was celebrated for the first time.

*Hint: The year 1995 was not a leap year since it is not divisible by $4.$*" :question/worked-solution "We can solve this problem using modular arithmetic.

First, we note the number of complete months between January 1st, 1995, and September 1st, 1995. 

- There were $5$ months with $31$ days (January, March, May, July,  and  August).

- There were $2$ months with $30$ days (April and  June).

- There was $1$ month with $28$ days (February).

Therefore, the number of days $d$ between January 1st and September 19th is given by

$$
d=\overset{\text{days to September 1st}}{\overset{⏞}{31(5)+30(2)+28(1)}}+18.
$$

Now, note that

$$
31≡3,\,30≡2,\,28≡0,\,18≡4\,(\text{mod}\,7).
$$

Therefore, writing the number $d$ modulo $7,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =5(31)+2(30)+1(28)+18 \\  & ≡5(3)+2(2)+1(0)+4\, & (\text{mod}\,7) \\  & ≡15+4+0+4\, & (\text{mod}\,7) \\  & ≡1+4+0+4\, & (\text{mod}\,7) \\  & ≡9\, & (\text{mod}\,7) \\  & ≡2\, & (\text{mod}\,7)\end{aligned}
$$

First, we note the number of complete months between January 1st, 1600, and October 1st, 1600. 

- There were $5$ months with $31$ days (January, March, May, July, and August).

- There were $3$ months with $30$ days (April, June, and September).

- There was $1$ month with $29$ days (February).

Therefore, the number of days $d$ between January 1st and October 6th is given by

$$
d=\overset{\text{days to October 1st}}{\overset{⏞}{31(5)+30(3)+29(1)}}+5.
$$

Now, note that

$$
31≡3,\,30≡2,\,29≡1,\,5≡5,\,(\text{mod}\,7).
$$

Therefore, writing the number $d$ modulo $7,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =5(31)+3(30)+1(29)+5 \\  & ≡5(3)+3(2)+(1)+5\, & (\text{mod}\,7) \\  & ≡15+6+1+5\, & (\text{mod}\,7) \\  & ≡1+6+1+5\, & (\text{mod}\,7) \\  & ≡13\, & (\text{mod}\,7) \\  & ≡6\, & (\text{mod}\,7)\end{aligned}
$$

Moreover, $a$ and $b$ are congruent modulo $n$ if and only if $n$ divides $a-b.$

$$
a \equiv b \quad (\textrm{mod}\,n) \qquad \Longleftrightarrow \qquad n \mid (a-b) \qquad \Longleftrightarrow \qquad a-b = kn,
$$

where $k\in\mathbb Z.$ 

A convenient property of congruences is that we can add and subtract on both sides, just as with regular equations. 

Consider, for instance, the following true statement:

$$
22\equiv 10 \quad (\textrm{mod}\,12)
$$

The **addition property** allows us to add an integer to both sides. For example, adding $2$ to both sides gives

$$
\begin{aligned}22+2 & ≡10+2\, & (\text{mod}\,12) \\ 24 & ≡12\, & (\text{mod}\,12)\end{aligned}
$$

which is also a true statement since $24$ and $12$ both have a remainder of zero when divided by $12.$

Similarly, the **subtraction property** allows us to subtract an integer from both sides. For example, subtracting $9$ from both sides of our original statement gives

$$
\begin{aligned}22-9 & ≡10-9\, & (\text{mod}\,12) \\ 13 & ≡1\, & (\text{mod}\,12)\end{aligned}
$$

which is a true statement since $13$ and $1$ both have a remainder of $1$ when divided by $12.$

In general, the addition and subtraction properties state the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}a≡b\,⟺\,a+c≡b+c\,(\text{mod}\,n) \\ a≡b\,⟺\,a-c≡b-c\,(\text{mod}\,n)\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186153447 :tutorial/content "According to the definition of modular congruence, we have that

$$
a \equiv b \quad (\textrm{mod}\,n) \qquad \Longleftrightarrow \qquad n \mid (a-b)  \qquad \Longleftrightarrow \qquad a = b+ kn,
$$

where $k \in \mathbb{Z}.$ Substituting $b=0,$ we obtain

$$
a \equiv 0 \quad (\textrm{mod}\,n) \qquad \Longleftrightarrow \qquad n \mid a  \qquad \Longleftrightarrow \qquad a = kn
$$

This gives rise to the following important fact:

*Any integer multiple of $n$ is congruent to $0$ modulo $n.$*

For example, the numbers $10,$ $-25,$ and $75$ are all are all multiples of ${\color{blue}5},$ so they are all congruent to $0$ modulo ${\color{blue}5}\mathbin{:}$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}10 & =2\cdot 5≡0 & \,(\text{mod}\,5) \\ -25 & =(-5)\cdot 5≡0 & \,(\text{mod}\,5) \\ 75 & =15\cdot 5≡0 & \,(\text{mod}\,5)\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186153450 :tutorial/content "Let's try to simplify the right-hand side of the following congruence:

$$
x \equiv 102 \quad (\textrm{mod}\,5)
$$

By "simplify," we mean that we wish to transform the number on the right-hand side to be the smallest possible positive integer. In other words, we want to write

$$
x \equiv r \quad (\textrm{mod}\,5)\qquad\textrm{for}\qquad 0 \leq r < 5.
$$

When we add $0$ to both sides of a congruence modulo $n$, we can form an equivalent congruence by writing $0$ as an integer multiple of $n.$ This works because every integer multiple of $n$ is congruent to $0\:(\textrm{mod}\:{\color{black}n}).$ 

In our case, we add zero to both sides of the congruence and then use the fact that  ${\color{blue}5} \cdot (-20) \equiv 0 \: (\text{mod}\:{\color{blue}5})$ to rewrite the right-hand side, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ≡102\, & (\text{mod}\,5) \\ x+0 & ≡102+0\, & (\text{mod}\,5) \\ x & \text{ }≡102+5\cdot (-20)\, & (\text{mod}\,5) \\ x & ≡102-100\, & (\text{mod}\,5) \\ x & ≡2\, & (\text{mod}\,5)\end{aligned}
$$

We conclude that $x \equiv 102\, (\textrm{mod}\,5)$ is equivalent to $x \equiv 2\, (\textrm{mod}\,5).$

Our answer is correct because $102$ and $2$ both have a remainder of $2$ when divided by $5,$ and $0 \leq  2 < 5.$

**Note:** By the division algorithm, there is exactly one value of $r$ that satisfies

$$
x \equiv r \quad (\textrm{mod}\,n)\qquad\textrm{for}\qquad 0 \leq r < n.
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186153472 :tutorial/content "In this lesson, we've been working with the so-called addition property of modular arithmetic.

$$
a\equiv b  \quad \Longleftrightarrow\quad a+c\equiv b+c \qquad (\textrm{mod}\,n)
$$

It's straightforward to prove the addition property by writing $a\equiv b$ in terms of divisibility:

$$
\begin{aligned}a≡b\,(\text{mod}\,n)\, & ⟺\,a-b=kn \\  & ⟺\,(a+c)-(b+c)=kn \\  & ⟺\,(a+c)≡(b+c)\,(\text{mod}\,n)\end{aligned}
$$

The subtraction property is proved similarly:

$$
\begin{aligned}a≡b\,(\text{mod}\,n)\, & ⟺\,a-b=kn \\  & ⟺\,(a-c)-(b-c)=kn \\  & ⟺\,(a-c)≡(b-c)\,(\text{mod}\,n)\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186152340 :activity/expected-seconds 600.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]}] "assertions" [[17592186151834 :question/problem "If $x + 8 \equiv 11\: (\textrm{mod}\,15),$ find an equivalent statement where $x$ is isolated."] [17592186151834 :question/worked-solution "The addition property of congruences states that 

$$
a\equiv b  \quad \Longleftrightarrow\quad a+c\equiv b+c \qquad (\textrm{mod}\,n).
$$

Similarly, the subtraction property states that

$$
a\equiv b \quad \Longleftrightarrow\quad a-c\equiv b-c \qquad (\textrm{mod}\,n).
$$

We use the subtraction property to subtract $8$ from both sides of the given congruence, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x+8 & ≡11\, & (\text{mod}\,15) \\ x+8-8 & ≡11-8\, & (\text{mod}\,15) \\ x & ≡3\, & (\text{mod}\,15)\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186151836 :question/problem "Which of the following numbers is congruent to $0$ modulo $18?$

- $-45$

- $42$

- $-54$"] [17592186151836 :question/worked-solution "First, recall that  

$$
a \equiv 0 \quad (\textrm{mod}\,n) \qquad \Longleftrightarrow \qquad a = kn,
$$

where $k\in\mathbb Z.$ In other words, when $a$ is divided by $n,$ there is no remainder. This means that any integer multiple of $18$ is congruent to $0$ modulo $18.$

So, since $18\,|\,(-54),$ we obtain

$$
-54 \equiv (-3) \cdot {\color{blue}18} \equiv (-3)\cdot 0\equiv 0 \quad (\text{mod}\:{\color{blue}18}).
$$

None of the other options are multiples of $18.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only.""] [17592186151839 :question/problem "Which of the following is equivalent to $x \equiv 23\: (\textrm{mod}\,6)?$ 

- $x \equiv 2 \quad (\textrm{mod}\,6)$

- $x \equiv 3 \quad (\textrm{mod}\,6)$

- $x \equiv 5 \quad (\textrm{mod}\,6)$"] [17592186151839 :question/worked-solution "When we add zero to both sides of a congruence modulo $n$, we can form an equivalent congruence by writing zero as an integer multiple of $n.$ This works because every integer multiple of $n$ is congruent to zero modulo $n.$

$$

:question/problem "Which of the following is congruent to $0$ modulo $14?$"] ["question-6d54f83a-3712-59c6-b238-0e2bb4334321" :question/worked-solution "First, recall that 

$$
a≡0\,(\text{mod}\,n)\,⟺\,a=kn,
$$

where $k\in Z.$ In other words, when $a$ is divided by $n,$ there is no remainder. This means that any integer multiple of $14$ is congruent to $0$ modulo $14.$

Therefore, since $14\,|\,(-84),$ we obtain

$$
-84≡(-6)\cdot 14≡(-6)\cdot 0≡0\,(\text{mod}\,14).
$$

None of the other options are multiples of $14.$"] ["question-6d54f83a-3712-59c6-b238-0e2bb4334321" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] First, we note the number of complete months between January 1st, 1995, and September 1st, 1995. 

- There were $5$ months with $31$ days (January, March, May, July,  and  August).

- There were $2$ months with $30$ days (April and  June).

- There was $1$ month with $28$ days (February).

Therefore, the number of days $d$ between January 1st and September 19th is given by

$$
d=\overset{\text{days to September 1st}}{\overset{⏞}{31(5)+30(2)+28(1)}}+18.
$$

Now, note that

$$
31≡3,\,30≡2,\,28≡0,\,18≡4\,(\text{mod}\,7).
$$

Therefore, writing the number $d$ modulo $7,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =5(31)+2(30)+1(28)+18 \\  & ≡5(3)+2(2)+1(0)+4\, & (\text{mod}\,7) \\  & ≡15+4+0+4\, & (\text{mod}\,7) \\  & ≡1+4+0+4\, & (\text{mod}\,7) \\  & ≡9\, & (\text{mod}\,7) \\  & ≡2\, & (\text{mod}\,7)\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the day of the week is the same as the date $2$ days after January 1st, 1995, namely Tuesday."] ["question-700ec10d-3e3a-58fc-aadf-2fee69932797" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] - There were $3$ months with $30$ days (April, June, and September).

- There was $1$ month with $29$ days (February).

$$
d=\overset{\text{days to October 1st}}{\overset{⏞}{31(5)+30(3)+29(1)}}+5.
$$

Now, note that

$$
31≡3,\,30≡2,\,29≡1,\,5≡5,\,(\text{mod}\,7).
$$

Therefore, writing the number $d$ modulo $7,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =5(31)+3(30)+1(29)+5 \\  & ≡5(3)+3(2)+(1)+5\, & (\text{mod}\,7) \\  & ≡15+6+1+5\, & (\text{mod}\,7) \\  & ≡1+6+1+5\, & (\text{mod}\,7) \\  & ≡13\, & (\text{mod}\,7) \\  & ≡6\, & (\text{mod}\,7)\end{aligned}
$$

- There is $1$ month with $28$ days (February).

$$
d=\overset{\text{days to December 1st}}{\overset{⏞}{31(6)+30(4)+28(1)}}+24.
$$

Now, note that

$$
31≡3,\,30≡2,\,28≡0,\,24≡3\,(\text{mod}\,7).
$$

Therefore, writing the number $d$ modulo $7,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =6(31)+4(30)+1(28)+24 \\  & ≡6(3)+4(2)+(0)+3\, & (\text{mod}\,7) \\  & ≡18+8+0+3\, & (\text{mod}\,7) \\  & ≡4+1+0+3\, & (\text{mod}\,7) \\  & ≡8\, & (\text{mod}\,7) \\  & ≡1\, & (\text{mod}\,7)\end{aligned}
$$

["question-83693413-601d-53f0-b546-e5ed9a2ee614" :question/math-academy-id "q-213292"] ["question-83693413-601d-53f0-b546-e5ed9a2ee614" :question/problem "On November 16th, 1700, Spain's King Charles II died. Given that January 1st, 1700, was a Friday, use congruences to determine on which day of the week Charles II died.

*Hint: The year 1700 was not a leap year since it's an end-of-century year (multiple of $100$) and is not divisible by $400.$*"] ["question-83693413-601d-53f0-b546-e5ed9a2ee614" :question/worked-solution "We can solve this problem using modular arithmetic.

First, we note the number of complete months between January 1st, 1700, and November 1st, 1700. 

- There were $6$ months with $31$ days (January, March, May, July, August, and October).

- There were $3$ months with $30$ days (April, June, and September).

- There was $1$ month with $28$ days (February).

Therefore, the number of days $d$ between January 1st and November 16th is given by

$$
d=\overset{\text{days to November 1st}}{\overset{⏞}{31(6)+30(3)+28(1)}}+15.
$$

Now, note that

$$
31≡3,\,30≡2,\,28≡0,\,15≡1\,(\text{mod}\,7).
$$

Therefore, writing the number $d$ modulo $7,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =6(31)+3(30)+1(28)+15 \\  & ≡6(3)+3(2)+(0)+1\, & (\text{mod}\,7) \\  & ≡18+6+0+1\, & (\text{mod}\,7) \\  & ≡4+6+0+1\, & (\text{mod}\,7) \\  & ≡11\, & (\text{mod}\,7) \\  & ≡4\, & (\text{mod}\,7)\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the day of the week is the same as the date $4$ days after January 1st, 1700, namely Tuesday."] ["question-83693413-601d-53f0-b546-e5ed9a2ee614" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] "question-5f92504f-2a88-577a-b7ee-007131f73594"] [17592186153446 :tutorial/content "Recall that two integers $a$ and $b$ are *congruent modulo* $n$ if they have the same remainder when divided by $n.$

Moreover, $a$ and $b$ are congruent modulo $n$ if and only if $n$ divides $a-b.$

$$
a \equiv b \quad (\textrm{mod}\,n) \qquad \Longleftrightarrow \qquad n \mid (a-b) \qquad \Longleftrightarrow \qquad a-b = kn,
$$

where $k\in\mathbb Z.$ 

A convenient property of congruences is that we can add and subtract on both sides, just as with regular equations. 

Consider, for instance, the following true statement:

$$
22\equiv 10 \quad (\textrm{mod}\,12)
$$

The **addition property** allows us to add an integer to both sides. For example, adding $2$ to both sides gives

$$
\begin{aligned}22+2 & ≡10+2\, & (\text{mod}\,12) \\ 24 & ≡12\, & (\text{mod}\,12)\end{aligned}
$$

which is also a true statement since $24$ and $12$ both have a remainder of zero when divided by $12.$

Similarly, the **subtraction property** allows us to subtract an integer from both sides. For example, subtracting $9$ from both sides of our original statement gives

$$
\begin{aligned}22-9 & ≡10-9\, & (\text{mod}\,12) \\ 13 & ≡1\, & (\text{mod}\,12)\end{aligned}
$$

which is a true statement since $13$ and $1$ both have a remainder of $1$ when divided by $12.$

In general, the addition and subtraction properties state the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}a≡b\,⟺\,a+c≡b+c\,(\text{mod}\,n) \\ a≡b\,⟺\,a-c≡b-c\,(\text{mod}\,n)\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186153447 :tutorial/content "According to the definition of modular congruence, we have that

$$
a \equiv b \quad (\textrm{mod}\,n) \qquad \Longleftrightarrow \qquad n \mid (a-b)  \qquad \Longleftrightarrow \qquad a = b+ kn,
$$

where $k \in \mathbb{Z}.$ Substituting $b=0,$ we obtain

$$
a \equiv 0 \quad (\textrm{mod}\,n) \qquad \Longleftrightarrow \qquad n \mid a  \qquad \Longleftrightarrow \qquad a = kn
$$

This gives rise to the following important fact:

*Any integer multiple of $n$ is congruent to $0$ modulo $n.$*

For example, the numbers $10,$ $-25,$ and $75$ are all are all multiples of ${\color{blue}5},$ so they are all congruent to $0$ modulo ${\color{blue}5}\mathbin{:}$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}10 & =2\cdot 5≡0 & \,(\text{mod}\,5) \\ -25 & =(-5)\cdot 5≡0 & \,(\text{mod}\,5) \\ 75 & =15\cdot 5≡0 & \,(\text{mod}\,5)\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186153450 :tutorial/content "Let's try to simplify the right-hand side of the following congruence:

$$
x \equiv 102 \quad (\textrm{mod}\,5)
$$

By "simplify," we mean that we wish to transform the number on the right-hand side to be the smallest possible positive integer. In other words, we want to write

$$
x \equiv r \quad (\textrm{mod}\,5)\qquad\textrm{for}\qquad 0 \leq r < 5.
$$

When we add $0$ to both sides of a congruence modulo $n$, we can form an equivalent congruence by writing $0$ as an integer multiple of $n.$ This works because every integer multiple of $n$ is congruent to $0\:(\textrm{mod}\:{\color{black}n}).$ 

In our case, we add zero to both sides of the congruence and then use the fact that  ${\color{blue}5} \cdot (-20) \equiv 0 \: (\text{mod}\:{\color{blue}5})$ to rewrite the right-hand side, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ≡102\, & (\text{mod}\,5) \\ x+0 & ≡102+0\, & (\text{mod}\,5) \\ x & \text{ }≡102+5\cdot (-20)\, & (\text{mod}\,5) \\ x & ≡102-100\, & (\text{mod}\,5) \\ x & ≡2\, & (\text{mod}\,5)\end{aligned}
$$

We conclude that $x \equiv 102\, (\textrm{mod}\,5)$ is equivalent to $x \equiv 2\, (\textrm{mod}\,5).$

Our answer is correct because $102$ and $2$ both have a remainder of $2$ when divided by $5,$ and $0 \leq  2 < 5.$

**Note:** By the division algorithm, there is exactly one value of $r$ that satisfies

$$
x \equiv r \quad (\textrm{mod}\,n)\qquad\textrm{for}\qquad 0 \leq r < n.
$$"] [17592186153472 :tutorial/content "In this lesson, we've been working with the so-called addition property of modular arithmetic.

$$
a\equiv b  \quad \Longleftrightarrow\quad a+c\equiv b+c \qquad (\textrm{mod}\,n)
$$

It's straightforward to prove the addition property by writing $a\equiv b$ in terms of divisibility:

$$
\begin{aligned}a≡b\,(\text{mod}\,n)\, & ⟺\,a-b=kn \\  & ⟺\,(a+c)-(b+c)=kn \\  & ⟺\,(a+c)≡(b+c)\,(\text{mod}\,n)\end{aligned}
$$

The subtraction property is proved similarly:

$$
\begin{aligned}a≡b\,(\text{mod}\,n)\, & ⟺\,a-b=kn \\  & ⟺\,(a-c)-(b-c)=kn \\  & ⟺\,(a-c)≡(b-c)\,(\text{mod}\,n)\end{aligned}

$$
a \equiv b \quad (\textrm{mod}\,n) \qquad \Longleftrightarrow \qquad n \mid (a-b) \qquad \Longleftrightarrow \qquad a-b = kn

where $k\in\mathbb Z$.

Consider, for instance, the following true statement:

$$

$$

The **addition property** allows us to add an integer to both sides. For example, adding $2$ to both sides gives

$$
\begin{bmatrix}22 + 2 & ≡10 + 2 & (mod12) \\ 24 & ≡12 & (mod12)\end{bmatrix}
$$

which is also a true statement since $24$ and $12$ both have a remainder of zero when divided by $12$.

$$
\begin{bmatrix}22 - 9 & ≡10 - 9 & (mod12) \\ 13 & ≡1 & (mod12)\end{bmatrix}
$$

which is a true statement since $13$ and $1$ both have a remainder of $1$ when divided by $12$.

$$"] [17592186153447 :tutorial/content "According to the definition of modular congruence, we have that

$$

> *Any integer multiple of $n$ is congruent to $0$ modulo $n$.*

$$

$$

$$

We conclude that $x \equiv 102\, (\textrm{mod}\,5)$ is equivalent to $x \equiv 2\, (\textrm{mod}\,5)$.

Our answer is correct because $102$ and $2$ both have a remainder of $2$ when divided by $5$, and

$$

$$"] [17592186153472 :tutorial/content "In this lesson, we've been working with the so-called addition property of modular arithmetic.

It's straightforward to prove the addition property by writing $a\equiv b$ in terms of divisibility:

$$

$$"]]}

:knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186152061 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "ea9b0644-090a-52a4-bc21-18fee98acbd3" :knowledge-point/title "Date Problems"}] :question/problem "The opening ceremony of the first modern Olympic Games was held on April 6th, 1896. Given that January 1st, 1896, was a Wednesday, use congruences to determine the day on which the Olympic Games opened.

*Hint: The year 1896 was a leap year since it's divisible by $4$ and is not an end-of-century year.*" :question/worked-solution "We can solve this problem using modular arithmetic.

First, we note the number of complete months between January 1st, 1896, and April 6th, 1896.

- There were $2$ months with $31$ days (January and March).
- There were $0$ months with $30$ days.
- There was $1$ month with $29$ days (February) since it was a leap year.

Therefore, the number of days $d$ between January 1st and April 6th is given by

$$
d = \overbrace{31(2) + 30(0) + 29(1)}^{\textrm{days to April 1st}} + 5
$$

Now, note that
$31 \equiv 3, \qquad 30\equiv 2, \qquad 29\equiv 1 \qquad (\textrm{mod}\, 7)$.

Therefore, writing the number $d$ modulo $7$, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}
d &= 2(31) + 0(30) + 1(29) + 5 \\
&= ≡2(3) + 0(2) + 1(1) + 5\begin{vmatrix}(mod7) \\ ≡6 + 0 + 1 + 5\end{vmatrix}(mod7) \\
&= ≡12\begin{vmatrix}(mod7) \\ ≡5\end{vmatrix}(mod7)
\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the day of the week is the same as the date $5$ days after January 1st, 1896, namely Monday."} {:db/id 17592186152481 :question/id #uuid "35bbfc39-ec46-5081-a039-066e5953ba2a" :question/math-academy-id "q-212904" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186152061 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "ea9b0644-090a-52a4-bc21-18fee98acbd3" :knowledge-point/title "Date Problems"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "aaae508c-8d52-52ea-a754-8f06715c0a78" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "Tuesday" :db/id 17592186149461} {:answer/id #uuid "ca248ef5-ce1e-5e94-be87-6812c2f9b419" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "Monday" :db/id 17592186149462} {:answer/id #uuid "da43fa1e-8a78-5986-9c3f-919c49763b02" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "Wednesday" :db/id 17592186149463} {:answer/id #uuid "ec310019-57d4-5d7e-9146-2f9ab55804fc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "Sunday" :db/id 17592186149464} {:answer/id #uuid "59b957c3-92b5-5dad-a281-2719f1dc4a77" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "Saturday" :db/id 17592186149465}] :answer-field/id #uuid "eda67795-6345-5de5-9844-da7b8759050c" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186149460}] :question/problem "You're given that January 1st, 2000, was a Saturday. [{:db/id 17592186152893 :step/content {:db/id 17592186153446 :tutorial/content "Recall that two integers $a$ and $b$ are *congruent modulo* $n$ if they have the same remainder when divided by $n$.

Moreover, $a$ and $b$ are congruent modulo $n$ if and only if $n$ divides $a-b$.

$$
a \equiv b \quad (\textrm{mod}\,n) \qquad \Longleftrightarrow \qquad n \mid (a-b) \qquad \Longleftrightarrow \qquad a-b = kn
$$

where $k\in\mathbb Z$.

A convenient property of congruences is that we can add and subtract on both sides, just as with regular equations.

Consider, for instance, the following true statement:

$$
22\equiv 10 \quad (\textrm{mod}\,12)
$$

The **addition property** allows us to add an integer to both sides. For example, adding $2$ to both sides gives

$$
\begin{bmatrix}22 + 2 & ≡10 + 2 & (mod12) \\ 24 & ≡12 & (mod12)\end{bmatrix}
$$

which is also a true statement since $24$ and $12$ both have a remainder of zero when divided by $12$.

Similarly, the **subtraction property** allows us to subtract an integer from both sides. For example, subtracting $9$ from both sides of our original statement gives

$$
\begin{bmatrix}22 - 9 & ≡10 - 9 & (mod12) \\ 13 & ≡1 & (mod12)\end{bmatrix}
$$

which is a true statement since $13$ and $1$ both have a remainder of $1$ when divided by $12$.

In general, the addition and subtraction properties state the following:

$$
a≡b⟺a + c≡b + c(modn); a≡b⟺a - c≡b - c(modn)
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "4cfdbd62-6b93-54bb-ad88-40ac101afaad" :tutorial/math-academy-id 9012 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "59df1347-5830-5a1b-a7dd-84190b29fa90" :step/math-academy-id 129882 :step/next {:db/id 17592186152894}} {:db/id 17592186152894 :step/content {:db/id 17592186152058 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186151834 :question/id #uuid "38f80c3a-6e6e-503d-a015-7040edc622bd" :question/math-academy-id "e-14580"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "d2755c3f-e76f-5cf9-a498-333e7e98ea8d" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049004}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186152472} {:db/id 17592186152473}] :knowledge-point/title "Using the Addition and Subtraction Properties"} :step/id #uuid "f23b3d68-c651-533b-847d-d2baf963aeb1" :step/math-academy-id 129883 :step/next {:db/id 17592186152895}} {:db/id 17592186152895 :step/content {:db/id 17592186153447 :tutorial/content "According to the definition of modular congruence, we have that

$$
a \equiv b \quad (\textrm{mod}\,n) \qquad \Longleftrightarrow \qquad n \mid (a-b) \qquad \Longleftrightarrow \qquad a = b+ kn
$$

where $k \in \mathbb{Z}$. Substituting $b=0$, we obtain

$$
a \equiv 0 \quad (\textrm{mod}\,n) \qquad \Longleftrightarrow \qquad n \mid a \qquad \Longleftrightarrow \qquad a = kn
$$

This gives rise to the following important fact:

> *Any integer multiple of $n$ is congruent to $0$ modulo $n$.*

For example, the numbers $10$, $-25$, and $75$ are all are all multiples of ${\color{blue}5}$, so they are all congruent to $0$ modulo ${\color{blue}5}$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\begin{bmatrix}10 &= 2 \cdot 5≡0 & (mod5) \\ -25|= (-5) \cdot 5≡0 & (mod5) \\ 75|= 15 \cdot 5≡0 & (mod5)\end{bmatrix}
\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "28b78d8b-aded-5d42-adda-0c07f20db3fa" :tutorial/math-academy-id 9013 :tutorial/title "Integers Congruent to Zero"} :step/id #uuid "4b3f7cd7-6397-59b0-999d-ac2990f23ca1" :step/math-academy-id 129887 :step/next {:db/id 17592186152896}} {:db/id 17592186152896 :step/content {:db/id 17592186152059 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186151836 :question/id #uuid "e379f1ee-3de3-56ad-8866-d9189f892704" :question/math-academy-id "e-14582"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "489ba3cf-c7da-5766-9638-2b5c5429d04c" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186152807} {:db/id 17592186152808}] :knowledge-point/title "Identifying Integers That Are Congruent to Zero Modulo N"} :step/id #uuid "101ac49e-3080-5f2b-9120-2dde89075a5c" :step/math-academy-id 129888 :step/next {:db/id 17592186152897}} {:db/id 17592186152897 :step/content {:db/id 17592186153450 :tutorial/content "Let's try to simplify the right-hand side of the following congruence:

$$
x \equiv 102 \quad (\textrm{mod}\,5)
$$

By "simplify," we mean that we wish to transform the number on the right-hand side to be the smallest possible positive integer. In other words, we want to write

$$
x \equiv r \quad (\textrm{mod}\,5)\qquad\textrm{for}\qquad 0 \leq r < 5
$$

When we add $0$ to both sides of a congruence modulo $n$, we can form an equivalent congruence by writing $0$ as an integer multiple of $n$. This works because every integer multiple of $n$ is congruent to $0\:(\textrm{mod}\:{\color{black}n})$.

In our case, we add zero to both sides of the congruence and then use the fact that ${\color{blue}5} \cdot (-20) \equiv 0 \: (\text{mod}\:{\color{blue}5})$ to rewrite the right-hand side, as follows:

$$
\begin{bmatrix}x & ≡102 & (mod5) \\ x + 0 & ≡102 + 0 & (mod5) \\ x & ≡102 + 5 \cdot (-20) & (mod5) \\ x & ≡102 - 100 & (mod5) \\ x & ≡2 & (mod5)\end{bmatrix}
$$

We conclude that $x \equiv 102\, (\textrm{mod}\,5)$ is equivalent to $x \equiv 2\, (\textrm{mod}\,5)$.

Our answer is correct because $102$ and $2$ both have a remainder of $2$ when divided by $5$, and

$$
0 \leq 2 < 5
$$

**Note:** By the division algorithm, there is exactly one value of $r$ that satisfies

$$
x \equiv r \quad (\textrm{mod}\,n)\qquad\textrm{for}\qquad 0 \leq r < n
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "abbf19fd-de43-5dd3-8007-2e6b8afda54a" :tutorial/math-academy-id 9016 :tutorial/title "Simplifying Congruences Using Integers Congruent to Zero"} :step/id #uuid "d7cc3e43-fac0-5489-9b4f-24b9546ae859" :step/math-academy-id 129891 :step/next {:db/id 17592186152898}} {:db/id 17592186152898 :step/content {:db/id 17592186152060 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186151839 :question/id #uuid "e92680c1-e40a-521d-b5b5-16a801e016ad" :question/math-academy-id "e-14585"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "7faa3c23-fa98-5c95-9c09-f0d489dbd472" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186152474} {:db/id 17592186152482}] :knowledge-point/title "Simplifying Congruences"} :step/id #uuid "a66be5cb-3b33-5cd4-969f-cc79d99883f9" :step/math-academy-id 129892 :step/next {:db/id 17592186152899}} {:db/id 17592186152899 :step/content {:db/id 17592186152061 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186151863 :question/id #uuid "1da5794f-02be-5a46-9450-d4b5611ee5a0" :question/math-academy-id "e-14646"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "ea9b0644-090a-52a4-bc21-18fee98acbd3" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186152481} {:db/id 17592186152494}] :knowledge-point/title "Date Problems"} :step/id #uuid "2687d1c2-403e-50c5-9c11-c27eb3dec9c3" :step/math-academy-id 129896 :step/next {:db/id 17592186152922}} {:db/id 17592186152922 :step/content {:db/id 17592186153472 :tutorial/content "In this lesson, we've been working with the so-called addition property of modular arithmetic.

$$
a\equiv b \quad \Longleftrightarrow\quad a+c\equiv b+c \qquad (\textrm{mod}\,n)
$$

It's straightforward to prove the addition property by writing $a\equiv b$ in terms of divisibility:

$$
a≡b(modn) \mid ⟺a - b = kn; ⟺(a + c) - (b + c) = kn; ⟺(a + c)≡(b + c)(modn)
$$

The subtraction property is proved similarly:

$$
a≡b(modn) \mid ⟺a - b = kn; ⟺(a - c) - (b - c) = kn; ⟺(a - c)≡(b - c)(modn)
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "99c9429f-482b-52c6-a194-aad63808d792" :tutorial/math-academy-id 9123 :tutorial/title "Proof of the Addition and Subtraction Properties"} :step/id #uuid "717075d8-24f1-5d84-948e-a60b9b4033eb" :step/math-academy-id 137432}] :activity/title "The Addition Property of Modular Arithmetic" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186152340} {:db/id 17592186152893 :step/content {:db/id 17592186153446 :tutorial/content "Recall that two integers $a$ and $b$ are *congruent modulo* $n$ if they have the same remainder when divided by $n$.

The **addition property** allows us to add an integer to both sides. For example, adding $2$ to both sides gives

$$
\begin{bmatrix}22 + 2 & ≡10 + 2 & (mod12) \\ 24 & ≡12 & (mod12)\end{bmatrix}
$$

which is also a true statement since $24$ and $12$ both have a remainder of zero when divided by $12$.

Similarly, the **subtraction property** allows us to subtract an integer from both sides. For example, subtracting $9$ from both sides of our original statement gives

$$
\begin{bmatrix}22 - 9 & ≡10 - 9 & (mod12) \\ 13 & ≡1 & (mod12)\end{bmatrix}
$$

which is a true statement since $13$ and $1$ both have a remainder of $1$ when divided by $12$.

In general, the addition and subtraction properties state the following:

$$
a≡b⟺a + c≡b + c(modn); a≡b⟺a - c≡b - c(modn)
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "4cfdbd62-6b93-54bb-ad88-40ac101afaad" :tutorial/math-academy-id 9012 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186152894 :step/content {:db/id 17592186152058 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186151834 :question/id #uuid "38f80c3a-6e6e-503d-a015-7040edc622bd" :question/math-academy-id "e-14580"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "d2755c3f-e76f-5cf9-a498-333e7e98ea8d" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049004}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186152472} {:db/id 17592186152473}] :knowledge-point/title "Using the Addition and Subtraction Properties"} :step/id #uuid "f23b3d68-c651-533b-847d-d2baf963aeb1" :step/math-academy-id 129883 :step/next {:db/id 17592186152895}} {:db/id 17592186152895 :step/content {:db/id 17592186153447 :tutorial/content "According to the definition of modular congruence, we have that

$$
a \equiv b \quad (\textrm{mod}\,n) \qquad \Longleftrightarrow \qquad n \mid (a-b) \qquad \Longleftrightarrow \qquad a = b+ kn
$$

where $k \in \mathbb{Z}$. Substituting $b=0$, we obtain

$$
a \equiv 0 \quad (\textrm{mod}\,n) \qquad \Longleftrightarrow \qquad n \mid a \qquad \Longleftrightarrow \qquad a = kn
$$

This gives rise to the following important fact:

> *Any integer multiple of $n$ is congruent to $0$ modulo $n$.*

For example, the numbers $10$, $-25$, and $75$ are all are all multiples of ${\color{blue}5}$, so they are all congruent to $0$ modulo ${\color{blue}5}$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\begin{bmatrix}10 &= 2 \cdot 5≡0 & (mod5) \\ -25|= (-5) \cdot 5≡0 & (mod5) \\ 75|= 15 \cdot 5≡0 & (mod5)\end{bmatrix}
\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "28b78d8b-aded-5d42-adda-0c07f20db3fa" :tutorial/math-academy-id 9013 :tutorial/title "Integers Congruent to Zero"} :step/id #uuid "4b3f7cd7-6397-59b0-999d-ac2990f23ca1" :step/math-academy-id 129887 :step/next {:db/id 17592186152896}} {:db/id 17592186153447 :tutorial/content "According to the definition of modular congruence, we have that

$$
x \equiv 102 \quad (\textrm{mod}\,5)
$$

By "simplify," we mean that we wish to transform the number on the right-hand side to be the smallest possible positive integer. In other words, we want to write

$$
x \equiv r \quad (\textrm{mod}\,5)\qquad\textrm{for}\qquad 0 \leq r < 5
$$

When we add $0$ to both sides of a congruence modulo $n$, we can form an equivalent congruence by writing $0$ as an integer multiple of $n$. This works because every integer multiple of $n$ is congruent to $0\:(\textrm{mod}\:{\color{black}n})$.

In our case, we add zero to both sides of the congruence and then use the fact that ${\color{blue}5} \cdot (-20) \equiv 0 \: (\text{mod}\:{\color{blue}5})$ to rewrite the right-hand side, as follows:

$$
\begin{bmatrix}x & ≡102 & (mod5) \\ x + 0 & ≡102 + 0 & (mod5) \\ x & ≡102 + 5 \cdot (-20) & (mod5) \\ x & ≡102 - 100 & (mod5) \\ x & ≡2 & (mod5)\end{bmatrix}
$$

We conclude that $x \equiv 102\, (\textrm{mod}\,5)$ is equivalent to $x \equiv 2\, (\textrm{mod}\,5)$.

Our answer is correct because $102$ and $2$ both have a remainder of $2$ when divided by $5$, and

$$
0 \leq 2 < 5
$$

**Note:** By the division algorithm, there is exactly one value of $r$ that satisfies

$$
x \equiv r \quad (\textrm{mod}\,n)\qquad\textrm{for}\qquad 0 \leq r < n
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "abbf19fd-de43-5dd3-8007-2e6b8afda54a" :tutorial/math-academy-id 9016 :tutorial/title "Simplifying Congruences Using Integers Congruent to Zero"} :step/id #uuid "d7cc3e43-fac0-5489-9b4f-24b9546ae859" :step/math-academy-id 129891 :step/next {:db/id 17592186152898}} {:db/id 17592186153450 :tutorial/content "Let's try to simplify the right-hand side of the following congruence:

17592186045417] [17592186046673 1008 "This course introduces students to proof-writing essentials, bridging the gap between pure problem-solving and constructing formal mathematical arguments. Students will formalize their understanding of logic, sets, and functions while delving into new concepts such as congruence, relations, and cardinality.
This course serves as ideal preparation for students wishing to pursue undergraduate studies in formal mathematical disciplines, including Discrete Mathematics, Abstract Algebra, and Real Analysis.
The prerequisite for Methods of Proof is single-variable calculus, which would be satisfied by completion of either Calculus II, AP Calculus BC, or Mathematical Foundations III." 17592186045417] [17592186046673 1009 "Students begin by mastering the basics of logic and logical operations, including statements, predicates, connectives, logical laws, logical equivalence, conditional and biconditional statements, quantifiers, inference, and formal and informal language. By solidifying their grasp of these logical fundamentals, students will have a secure underpinning that enables them to embark on their journey into proof-writing confidently.
A robust knowledge of set theory is another cornerstone of mathematical proof-writing. Students will extend and formalize their understanding of sets and learn to translate between logical and set operations. By the end of the course, students will appreciate how set theory provides a comprehensive toolkit for proving mathematical results.
After mastering these fundamentals, students will explore various proof-writing techniques, including direct proof, proof by cases, proof by contrapositive, proof by contradiction, disproof, and mathematical induction. The course emphasizes proving concepts related to parity, divisibility, congruence, sequences, functions, set identities, and relations. Students will have multiple opportunities to test and refine their proof construction and comprehension skills throughout the course and in varied contexts
This challenging yet engaging course helps students with strong mathematical foundations build a solid base for further progression into advanced undergraduate courses." 17592186045417] "Recall that two integers $a$ and $b$ are *congruent modulo* $n$ if they have the same remainder when divided by $n$.

Moreover, $a$ and $b$ are congruent modulo $n$ if and only if $n$ divides $a-b$.

$$
a \equiv b \quad (\textrm{mod}\,n) \qquad \Longleftrightarrow \qquad n \mid (a-b) \qquad \Longleftrightarrow \qquad a-b = kn
$$

where $k\in\mathbb Z$.

A convenient property of congruences is that we can add and subtract on both sides, just as with regular equations.

Consider, for instance, the following true statement:

$$
22\equiv 10 \quad (\textrm{mod}\,12)
$$

The **addition property** allows us to add an integer to both sides. For example, adding $2$ to both sides gives

$$
\begin{bmatrix}22 + 2 & ≡10 + 2 & (mod12) \\ 24 & ≡12 & (mod12)\end{bmatrix}
$$

which is also a true statement since $24$ and $12$ both have a remainder of zero when divided by $12$.

Similarly, the **subtraction property** allows us to subtract an integer from both sides. For example, subtracting $9$ from both sides of our original statement gives

$$
\begin{bmatrix}22 - 9 & ≡10 - 9 & (mod12) \\ 13 & ≡1 & (mod12)\end{bmatrix}
$$

which is a true statement since $13$ and $1$ both have a remainder of $1$ when divided by $12$.

In general, the addition and subtraction properties state the following:

$$
a≡b⟺a + c≡b + c(modn); a≡b⟺a - c≡b - c(modn)
$$" 17592186045417] [17592186153446 1065 9012 17592186045417] [17592186153446 1066 #uuid "4cfdbd62-6b93-54bb-ad88-40ac101afaad" 17592186045417] [17592186153446 1067 "Introduction" 17592186045417] [17592186153447 1064 "According to the definition of modular congruence, we have that

$$
a \equiv b \quad (\textrm{mod}\,n) \qquad \Longleftrightarrow \qquad n \mid (a-b) \qquad \Longleftrightarrow \qquad a = b+ kn
$$

where $k \in \mathbb{Z}$. Substituting $b=0$, we obtain

$$
a \equiv 0 \quad (\textrm{mod}\,n) \qquad \Longleftrightarrow \qquad n \mid a \qquad \Longleftrightarrow \qquad a = kn
$$

This gives rise to the following important fact:

> *Any integer multiple of $n$ is congruent to $0$ modulo $n$.*

For example, the numbers $10$, $-25$, and $75$ are all are all multiples of ${\color{blue}5}$, so they are all congruent to $0$ modulo ${\color{blue}5}$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\begin{bmatrix}10 &= 2 \cdot 5≡0 & (mod5) \\ -25|= (-5) \cdot 5≡0 & (mod5) \\ 75|= 15 \cdot 5≡0 & (mod5)\end{bmatrix}
\end{aligned}
$$" 17592186045417] [17592186153447 1065 9013 17592186045417] [17592186153447 1066 #uuid "28b78d8b-aded-5d42-adda-0c07f20db3fa" 17592186045417] [17592186153447 1067 "Integers Congruent to Zero" 17592186045417] [17592186153450 1064 "Let's try to simplify the right-hand side of the following congruence:

$$
x \equiv 102 \quad (\textrm{mod}\,5)
$$

By "simplify," we mean that we wish to transform the number on the right-hand side to be the smallest possible positive integer. In other words, we want to write

$$
x \equiv r \quad (\textrm{mod}\,5)\qquad\textrm{for}\qquad 0 \leq r < 5
$$

When we add $0$ to both sides of a congruence modulo $n$, we can form an equivalent congruence by writing $0$ as an integer multiple of $n$. This works because every integer multiple of $n$ is congruent to $0\:(\textrm{mod}\:{\color{black}n})$.

In our case, we add zero to both sides of the congruence and then use the fact that ${\color{blue}5} \cdot (-20) \equiv 0 \: (\text{mod}\:{\color{blue}5})$ to rewrite the right-hand side, as follows:

$$
\begin{bmatrix}x & ≡102 & (mod5) \\ x + 0 & ≡102 + 0 & (mod5) \\ x & ≡102 + 5 \cdot (-20) & (mod5) \\ x & ≡102 - 100 & (mod5) \\ x & ≡2 & (mod5)\end{bmatrix}
$$

We conclude that $x \equiv 102\, (\textrm{mod}\,5)$ is equivalent to $x \equiv 2\, (\textrm{mod}\,5)$.

Our answer is correct because $102$ and $2$ both have a remainder of $2$ when divided by $5$, and

$$
0 \leq 2 < 5
$$

**Note:** By the division algorithm, there is exactly one value of $r$ that satisfies

$$
x \equiv r \quad (\textrm{mod}\,n)\qquad\textrm{for}\qquad 0 \leq r < n
$$" 17592186045417] [17592186153450 1065 9016 17592186045417] [17592186153450 1066 #uuid "abbf19fd-de43-5dd3-8007-2e6b8afda54a" 17592186045417] [17592186153450 1067 "Simplifying Congruences Using Integers Congruent to Zero" 17592186045417] [17592186153472 1064 "In this lesson, we've been working with the so-called addition property of modular arithmetic.

$$
a\equiv b \quad \Longleftrightarrow\quad a+c\equiv b+c \qquad (\textrm{mod}\,n)

It's straightforward to prove the addition property by writing $a\equiv b$ in terms of divisibility:
